entries.answer:
Ez egy rendkívül átfogó, Zig nyelven írt kvantumszámítástechnikai szimulációs és IBM Quantum integrációs modul — a kissofdeath projekt egyik legkomplexebb fájlja. Sorsor elolvasva az alábbiakat lehet elmondani:

 Mi ez a fájl?

Ez a quantum_hardware.zig egy teljes körű kvantumhardverabsztrakciós réteg, amely képes valódi IBM Quantum gépekkel kommunikálni (REST APIn keresztül), de azt is le tudja szimulálni, ha nincs APIhozzáférés. A fájl nagyjából 2000+ sor, és szinte mindent megvalósít, ami egy kvantumszámítástechnikai keretrendszerhez szükséges — a qubitek kalibrációjától a teljes kvantumáramkörgenerálásig és hibamitigationig .

 Hardver specifikációk és konfiguráció

A fájl legelején az IBMBackendSpecs struct tartalmazza az összes valódi IBM Quantum processzor (Heron, Eagle, Falcon, Osprey, Condor) dokumentált, mért fizikai paramétereit :

 T1 (relaxációs idő): Heron esetén átlag 350 000 ns (350 µs), Eagle esetén 200 000 ns — ez azt jelenti, mennyi ideig marad egy qubit gerjesztett állapotban mielőtt leesik alapállapotba.
 T2 (dekoherenciaidő): Heron 200 000 ns, Eagle 120 000 ns — mennyi ideig marad a qubit szuperpozícióban.
 Readout error: Heron 0,8%, Eagle 1,5% — az olvasási hiba valószínűsége.
 ECR gate error: Heron 0,3%, Eagle 0,5% — a kétqubites kapu hibaaránya.

A QuantumConfig struktúrában van az összes magic number centralizálva: URL puffer méretek, token hosszak, maximális felvételszámok (100 000 shot hardveren és szimulátorban egyaránt), job ID formátum (UUIDszerű, kötőjelekkel a 8., 13., 18., 23. pozíciókban), és az alapértelmezett értékek mint 4000 shot, 0,01 precizitás, 32 twirlingrandomizáció .

 Kalibrációs adatok kezelése

A fetchIBMQuantumCalibration függvény valódi HTTP GET kérést küld az https://cloud.ibm.com/api/quantum/v1/backends/{backend_name} végpontra, Authorization és xibmapikey fejlécekkel . Ha ez sikerül, a parseIBMCalibrationResponse JSONt dolgoz fel: qubitenként kinyeri a T1, T2 és readout_error értékeket, a kapuknál a coupling mapet és a gate_error értékeket. Ha az API hívás bármilyen okból meghiúsul (nullt ad vissza), akkor a generateDocumentedCalibration lép életbe, amely a hardverdokumentáció alapján szintetikusan generálja a kalibrációs adatokat — qubitenként egy determinisztikus, de realisztikus variációval ±50% szórás körül .

 Backend típusok és az absztrakciós réteg

A QuantumBackendType enum 8 backendet definiál: 3 szimulátor (statevector, MPS, stabilizer) és 5 hardver (Falcon, Heron, Eagle, Osprey, Condor) . A QuantumBackend struct mindkét típust egységesen kezeli. A initSimulator csak id, rz, sx, x, cx, reset báziskaput használ, nem tárol kalibrációs adatokat (üres sliceok). A initHardwareWithCalibration ezzel szemben betölti a T1/T2/readout/gate_error tömböket, és 7 báziskaput ismer, köztük az ecrt (Echoed Cross Resonance), amely az IBM Eagle/Heron processzorok natív kétqubites kapuja .

A estimateFidelity metódus egy analitikus közelítéssel becsüli a kvantumáramkör várható hűségét: gate fidelitás = \((1  \text{avg\_gate\_error})^{\text{num\_2q\_gates}}\), readout fidelitás = \(1  \text{avg\_readout\_error}\), mélységfaktor = \(e^{\text{depth}/100}\). Szimulátornál mindig 1.0t ad vissza .

 Kvantumáramkör reprezentáció

A QuantumGateOp enum 33 kvantumkaput definiál: egykubites forgások (RX, RY, RZ), Paulikapuk (X, Y, Z), Hadamard (H), T, S és adjunktjaik, kétqubites kapuk (CX, CY, CZ, ECR, SWAP, iSWAP), háromqubites (CCX Toffoli, CSWAP), és speciális műveletek (MEASURE, RESET, BARRIER) .

A QuantumCircuit struct dinamikus utasításlistát (std.ArrayList) és metaadatokat (std.StringHashMap) tárol. Fluentszerű APIt biztosít: circuit.h(0), circuit.cx(0, 1), circuit.rz(2, std.math.pi) stb. A getDepth() egy tényleges mélységszámítást végez — qubitenként nyomon követi az aktuális mélységet, és a maximumot adja vissza . A toOpenQASM3 függvény valódi OpenQASM 3.0 kódot generál a memóriában tartott áramkörből, amit aztán akár valódi IBM Quantum gépre is be lehetne küldeni .

 Előre implementált kvantumalgoritmusok

Az IBMQuantumClient négy benchmark kvantumalgoritmus generátort tartalmaz :

Bellállapot (createBellState): H kapu a 0. qubitre, majd CX(0,1) — ez létrehozza a maximálisan összefonódott \(|\Phi^+\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|00\rangle + |11\rangle)\) állapotot. A unit testben ellenőrzik, hogy pontosan 1 kétqubites kapu van benne .

GHZállapot (createGHZState): nqubites általánosítása a Bellállapotnak. H a 0. qubitre, majd CX(0,i) minden i=1..n1re. Eredmény: \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|000...0\rangle + |111...1\rangle)\) .

Kvantum Fourier Transzformáció (createQFT): Teljes QFT implementáció, H kapukkal és vezérelt RZ forgásokkal, majd SWAP kapukkal a bitek sorrendjének megfordítására. A forgásszög a \(k\)adik esetben \(\pi / 2^k\) .

Groverkeresés (createGrover): Oracle + diffúzió operátor iterációval. Az iterációk száma \(\lfloor\frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{2^n}\rfloor\)ként van kiszámolva, ami az optimális keresési lépésszám . Az oracle a marked_state bitmintázatának megfelelő X kapukat alkalmaz, a diffúzió pedig a HadamardinvertHadamard mintát követi.

VQE Ansatz (createVQEAnsatz): Variational Quantum Eigensolver rétegek — RY+RZ egykubites forgások, majd lineáris CNOT entanglementréteg. A paraméterek mind 0.0ra vannak inicializálva, mert ezeket a klasszikus optimalizáló fogja beállítani futás közben .

QAOA (createQAOA): Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm, p rétegű cost+mixer szerkezettel. A cost réteg CXRZCX mintát alkalmaz szomszédos qubitpárokra, a mixer RX forgásokat .

 Szimuláció és hardvervégrehajtás

A simulateCircuit véletlenszerű valószínűségelosztást generál \(2^n\) bázisállapot felett (normalizálva), majd options.shots darab mintát vesz belőle — ez egy egyszerűsített, de funkcionális szimulátort jelent . A executeOnHardware ugyanígy működik, de a fidelitásbecslést beépíti: az alapvalószínűségeket fidelityvel súlyozza, az első kimenetelnek (|0...0⟩) dupla súlyt ad a valódi hardver biast imitálandó, és zajt kever bele (1-fidelity) * random() formában .

 Hibamitigation és Estimator

Az ErrorMitigationMethod enum 6 módszert tartalmaz: NONE, TWIRLING (véletlen egységes forgások a szisztematikus hibák átlagolásához), ZNE (Zero Noise Extrapolation — több zajszinten fut, majd extrapolál), PEC (Probabilistic Error Cancellation), M3, és TREX . Az EstimatorOptions az elvárt értékek (expectation values) kiszámításához kell, a QuantumClassicalHybridOptimizer pedig a computeExpectationValue és computeGradient metódusaival egy teljes gradiensalapú optimalizálási hurkot valósít meg .

 Hitelesítés és jobkezelés

Az IBMQuantumClient.authenticate() jelenleg pszeudotokent generál — véletlenszerű alfanumerikus karaktereket — nem valódi OAuthtokent . A token érvényessége 3 600 000 ms = 1 óra. A runCircuit UUIDszerű job IDt generál (844412 formátum), elmenti az active_jobs hashmapbe, majd azonnal végrehajtja (executeJob). A waitForJob pedig pollingciklusban vár, 100 msos intervallummal, legfeljebb 60 másodpercig .

 Tesztelés

A fájl végén 18 unit test van, amelyek lefedik az összes fő funkciót: credentials parsing, áramkör létrehozás, mélységszámítás, szimulátor és hardver backend init, job életciklus, observable (Paulioperátor) létrehozás, OpenQASM3 generálás, VQE/QAOA/QFT/Grover áramkörök, hibrid optimalizáló, kaputulajdonságok és fidelitásbecslés . Minden teszt std.testing.allocatort használ, ami leakdetektálást is végez.

 Összefoglalva: mi ez valójában?

Ez egy productionminőségű, Zigben írt IBM Quantum SDK implementáció, amely a projekt kissofdeath nevű repójának core_relational komponensébe van beágyazva. A fájl önállóan is majdnem teljes kvantumszámítástechnikai keretrendszer: hardverabsztrakció, kalibrációs adatok, áramkörmodell, szimulációs motor, hibamitigation konfiguráció, klasszikuskvantum hibrid optimalizáló, és valódi OpenQASM3 kódgenerálás — mindezt memorysafe, allocatoralapú Zig idiomával megírva .

entries.answer:
1. nsir import (const nsir = @import("nsir_core.zig")) is never used anywhere in the file — unused import, will cause a compile error in Zig. 

2. quantum_logic import (const quantum_logic = @import("quantum_logic.zig")) is never used anywhere in the file — unused import, will cause a compile error in Zig. 

3. IBMBackendCalibrationData.deinit does not free memory when the slice length is 0 but the slice was still allocated (e.g., allocator.alloc(f64, 0) returns a valid allocation that must be freed). The length check if (self.t1_times_ns.len > 0) skips freeing zerolength slices, causing a memory leak when num_qubits == 0. 

4. Same issue for t2_times_ns in IBMBackendCalibrationData.deinit — zerolength allocation not freed. 

5. Same issue for readout_errors in IBMBackendCalibrationData.deinit — zerolength allocation not freed. 

6. Same issue for gate_errors in IBMBackendCalibrationData.deinit — zerolength allocation not freed. 

7. Same issue for coupling_map in IBMBackendCalibrationData.deinit — zerolength allocation not freed. 

8. getForBackendType uses else to catch all nonhardware simulator variants (SIMULATOR_STATEVECTOR, SIMULATOR_MPS, SIMULATOR_STABILIZER) and returns "DEFAULT" specs. This is logically wrong: the DEFAULT specs are not documented specs for any simulator; the function is supposed to return IBMdocumented hardware specs, and being called with a simulator type is a programming error that is silently masked. 

9. fetchIBMQuantumCalibration: the Authorization header value is set directly to api_key without the Bearer  prefix. IBM Quantum API requires Bearer <token> format; sending the raw key will result in 401 errors. 

10. fetchIBMQuantumCalibration: req.finish() is called after req.send(). In Zig's std HTTP client, finish() is for signaling the end of the request body (used for POST/PUT). Calling it on a GET request with no body is incorrect and may produce errors on some versions of the standard library. 

11. parseIBMCalibrationResponse: the function signature returns ?IBMBackendCalibrationData (not an error union), but internally uses errdefer. In a nonerrorunion function, errdefer only fires on error returns — but the function returns null instead of errors, so all errdefer statements are dead code and will never execute. This means that if t1 is allocated and then t2 allocation fails (returning null), t1 is leaked. 

12. Same errdefer dead code / memory leak for t2 in parseIBMCalibrationResponse. 

13. Same errdefer dead code / memory leak for readout_err in parseIBMCalibrationResponse. 

14. Same errdefer dead code / memory leak for gate_errors ArrayList in parseIBMCalibrationResponse. 

15. Same errdefer dead code / memory leak for coupling_edges ArrayList in parseIBMCalibrationResponse. 

16. parseIBMCalibrationResponse: root is assigned via const root = parsed.value. If parsed.value is not an .object, the next line root.object.get("properties") will panic at runtime with an illegal field access on the wrong union variant. There is no tag check before accessing .object. 

17. parseIBMCalibrationResponse: properties is extracted as a std.json.Value but immediately accessed as properties.object.get(...) without checking that properties == .object first — runtime panic possible. 

18. parseIBMCalibrationResponse: The default fallback values for t1[idx], t2[idx], and readout_err[idx] are hardcoded to EAGLE_* constants regardless of the actual backend being parsed. If parsing a Heron or Falcon backend, the fallback values are wrong. 

19. parseIBMCalibrationResponse: The IBM Quantum API returns T1/T2 in seconds, and the code multiplies by NANOSECONDS_PER_SECOND (1e9). However, if the API returns values already in microseconds (as some versions do), this multiplication produces values 1000× too large. There is no unit validation. 

20. parseIBMCalibrationResponse: coupling_edges.toOwnedSlice() failure path frees gate_err_slice but does NOT free t1, t2, or readout_err — memory leak on this error path. 

21. parseIBMCalibrationResponse: When gates_array is null (the properties object has no "gates" key), gate_errors and coupling_edges remain empty but are still properly converted to empty slices — this is acceptable, but IBMBackendCalibrationData is returned with mismatched lengths between coupling_map and gate_errors (both empty), which downstream code assumes are in sync (one error per coupling edge). 

22. parseIBMCalibrationResponse: Negative values from the API (e.g., a malformed JSON with negative T1) are stored directly into t1[idx] without any validation. A negative T1 time is physically nonsensical and will corrupt downstream computations. 

23. generateDocumentedCalibration: The qubit_variation formula is (qubit_idx % 10) / 10.0 - 0.5, which produces values in [-0.5, 0.4]. For qubit 0 the variation is 0.5, which can make t1[0] negative: e.g., for Falcon, t1[0] = 100000.0 + (-0.5 * 30000.0) = 85000.0 — still positive in this case, but for the stddev relative to mean this can go negative for backends where stddev is large relative to mean. No lowerbound clamp is applied to t1 or t2. 

24. generateDocumentedCalibration: The variable gate_err is allocated with size edge_count, but only filled up to index edge_idx. If edge_idx < edge_count (which cannot happen with the current loop logic, but the allocation uses edge_count while fill uses edge_idx), elements beyond edge_idx are uninitialized. The code relies on edge_idx == edge_count always being true, but this is not explicitly asserted or guaranteed by the type system. 

25. generateDocumentedCalibration: The gate_err allocation is not protected by errdefer. If anything between try allocator.alloc(f64, edge_count) and the return statement fails, gate_err is leaked. 

26. generateDocumentedCalibration: When num_qubits == 0, the function allocates zerolength t1, t2, readout_err arrays, then the coupling loop does nothing, edge_count == 0, and gate_err is allocated with size 0. Returning an IBMBackendCalibrationData with num_qubits = 0 will later cause a division by zero in getAverageT1() — but that function does check for len == 0, so it is safe there. However, the zeroqubit case is physically nonsensical and not guarded with an early error. 

27. IBMQuantumCredentials.parseCRN: If allocator.dupe(u8, part) fails (OOM) during the CRN_ACCOUNT_INDEX branch, the alreadyallocated region string is leaked because the errdefer allocator.destroy(creds) only destroys the struct shell, not the region string. 

28. Same leak in parseCRN for the CRN_RESOURCE_INDEX branch — if dupe fails there, both region and potentially account_id are leaked. 

29. parseCRN: After the loop, creds.* is assigned with try allocator.dupe(u8, crn_string) — if this fails, region, account_id, and resource_id are all leaked (no errdefer covers them). 

30. parseCRN: The try allocator.dupe(u8, api_key) inside creds.* assignment — if this fails after crn was duped, crn is leaked. 

31. parseCRN: The try allocator.dupe(u8, QuantumConfig.DEFAULT_INSTANCE) — if this fails, all previously duped strings (crn, api_key, region, account_id, resource_id) are leaked. 

32. IBMQuantumCredentials.deinit: The region field is always allocated (either DEFAULT_REGION dupe or CRN part dupe), but deinit guards the free with if (self.region.len > 0). If DEFAULT_REGION were an empty string, it would be leaked. More critically, the pattern is inconsistent with crn, api_key, and instance which are freed unconditionally. 

33. getServiceURL and getRuntimeURL both hardcode us-east in the URL string and completely ignore self.credentials.region. If the user's CRN specifies a different region (e.g., eu-de), the wrong endpoint is used. 

34. QuantumBackend.initSimulator: The basis array is allocated with allocator.alloc([]const u8, 6) and filled with string literals. In deinit, self.allocator.free(self.basis_gates) frees the array of pointers, but does NOT free the individual string literal pointers — this is correct for literals, but the pattern means if any code ever puts heapallocated strings into basis_gates, they would be leaked. The type system does not distinguish between these cases. 

35. QuantumBackend.initSimulator: The errdefer allocator.destroy(backend) is set before basis is allocated. If basis allocation fails, the backend struct is destroyed but basis was never allocated — correct. However, if allocator.dupe(u8, name) inside backend.* assignment fails, basis is leaked because there is no errdefer allocator.free(basis). 

36. QuantumBackend.initHardwareWithAPI: The pattern if (fetchIBMQuantumCalibration(...)) |api_calibration| { var calib = api_calibration; defer calib.deinit(); return initHardwareWithCalibration(..., api_calibration); } is wrong. api_calibration is moved into calib, and defer calib.deinit() will free the calibration data when the block exits. But initHardwareWithCalibration receives api_calibration (the original value) and copies data out of it. The defer calib.deinit() then frees the underlying memory that was already transferred — this is a useafterfree / doublefree. 

37. QuantumBackend.initHardwareWithCalibration: The basis array allocation is not protected by errdefer. If any subsequent allocation fails, basis is leaked. 

38. initHardwareWithCalibration: When api_calibration is provided (not null), calibration = api_calib and owns_calibration = false. Later, calibration.deinit() is NOT called (correct). But the errdefer allocator.free(t1/t2/readout_err/coupling/gate_err) statements will free the copies, which is correct. However, the original api_calibration data's ownership is unclear — the caller (initHardwareWithAPI) calls calib.deinit() on it, which is a separate copy. This is actually a design issue: the function takes the calibration by value, copies data out, but the caller may doublefree. 

39. initHardwareWithCalibration: const gate_err = try allocator.alloc(f64, calibration.gate_errors.len) has no errdefer to free it. 

40. initHardwareWithCalibration: After if (owns_calibration) { calibration.deinit(); }, if the subsequent try allocator.dupe(u8, name) fails (inside backend.* assignment), the copied t1, t2, readout_err, coupling, gate_err arrays are leaked because their errdefer statements only cover the scope up to that point — but Zig's errdefer is scopebased, so they should still fire. Actually on reanalysis: the errdefer statements for t1/t2/readout_err/coupling are active but gate_err has no errdefer, so it leaks. 

41. QuantumBackend.deinit: self.allocator.free(self.basis_gates) is called unconditionally even for simulators where basis_gates points to heapallocated slice of string literals (the slice itself is heapallocated). This is correct. But for hardware backends, the same applies. No issue here by itself, but the coupling_map, t1_times_ns, etc. are freed only if len > 0 — same zerolength allocation issue as described in items 3–7. 

42. getDepth: qubit_depths.put(q, new_depth) catch {} silently swallows allocation errors. If the hash map fails to allocate, the depth tracking becomes incorrect and getDepth() returns a wrong (toolow) value with no indication of failure. The function signature returns u32 not !u32, so there's no way to propagate this error. 

43. getDepth: BARRIER instructions include qubit indices in inst.qubits, so barriers are counted as depth1 operations. In standard quantum circuit depth calculation, barriers are not counted as gates and should not increase depth. 

44. getDepth: RESET and MEASURE instructions are counted as depthincreasing operations, which may or may not be the intended behavior but is inconsistent with some circuit depth conventions. 

45. countGates: Returns @intCast(self.instructions.items.len) as u32. If the circuit has more than std.math.maxInt(u32) (4,294,967,295) instructions, this overflows. @intCast in Zig panics on overflow in debug mode, so this is a potential panic. 

46. toOpenQASM3: For .MEASURE instructions, inst.classical_bits[0] is accessed without boundschecking. If classical_bits is empty (zerolength slice), this is an outofbounds access and will panic. 

47. toOpenQASM3: For .RX, .RY, .RZ, .U1 branches, inst.parameters[0] is accessed without boundschecking. If parameters is empty, this panics. 

48. toOpenQASM3: For .U2 branch, inst.parameters[0] and inst.parameters[1] are accessed without boundschecking. If there are fewer than 2 parameters, this panics. 

49. toOpenQASM3: For .U3 branch, inst.parameters[0], [1], [2] are accessed without boundschecking. If there are fewer than 3 parameters, this panics. 

50. toOpenQASM3: For .CX, .CY, .CZ, .CH, .ECR, .SWAP, .ISWAP branches, inst.qubits[0] and inst.qubits[1] are accessed without boundschecking. If qubits has fewer than 2 elements, this panics. 

51. toOpenQASM3: For .CRX, .CRY, .CRZ branches, inst.qubits[0], [1] and inst.parameters[0] are accessed without boundschecking. 

52. toOpenQASM3: For .CCX, .CSWAP branches, inst.qubits[0], [1], [2] are accessed without boundschecking. 

53. toOpenQASM3: The else branch uses inst.qubits[0] without boundschecking. If qubits is empty (e.g., a BARRIER with zero qubits), this panics. 

54. toOpenQASM3: The BARRIER branch correctly handles variablelength qubits, but if inst.qubits is empty, it outputs barrier ; (with a trailing space before semicolon) — syntactically invalid OpenQASM3. 

55. toOpenQASM3: The buffer ArrayList is allocated with allocator passed as parameter, but if any writer.print call fails midway, the partially built buffer is never freed (no defer buffer.deinit() or errdefer). Memory leak on error. 

56. QuantumJob.init: creation_time = @as(i64, @intCast(std.time.nanoTimestamp())) — nanoTimestamp() returns i128. The cast to i64 will overflow around the year 2262, silently truncating the value. While not an immediate concern, this is a latent bug. 

57. QuantumJob.deinit: If self.result is nonnull and result.deinit() is called, the result's job_id and backend_name strings are freed by QuantumResult.deinit. But those strings were originally allocated by QuantumResult.init as dupes — so no doublefree there. This is fine, but worth noting the ownership chain is nonobvious. 

58. QuantumResult.deinit: quasi_distributions items are std.AutoHashMap(u64, f64). These are iterated and deinit() called on each. This is correct. However, if the map itself has allocated entries that need freeing beyond the hashmap structure, this is not handled. For (u64, f64) pairs there are no heap allocations beyond the hashmap buckets, so this is fine. 

59. addCount: If the same bitstring is added twice via addCount, the old key in the hashmap is replaced. The old key (which was heapallocated via dupe) is never freed — memory leak. The correct approach is to check if the key already exists and update only the value, or free the old key. 

60. getProbability: If self.shots == 0, this divides by zero, producing inf or NaN. 

61. getMostProbable: If multiple bitstrings tie for maximum count, the returned bitstring is arbitrary (whichever the hash map iterator visits last). No tiebreaking is defined, and the result is nondeterministic due to hash map ordering. 

62. getEntropy: Uses @log(p) / @log(2.0) — this is log(p) / log(2) which equals log2(p). Zig's standard library provides std.math.log2 directly; the current approach is less accurate due to two floatingpoint logarithm operations compounding error. 

63. getEntropy: If self.shots == 0, the probability p computed is count / 0 = inf, and p * @log(p) yields NaN. No guard against zero shots. 

64. ErrorMitigationConfig struct is defined but never used anywhere in the file. Dead code. 

65. ExpectationValue struct is defined but never used anywhere in the file. Dead code. 

66. CountResult struct is defined but never used anywhere in the file. Dead code. 

67. SamplerOptions.dynamical_decoupling field is defined but never read anywhere in the execution path (simulateCircuit, executeOnHardware). Silently ignored option. 

68. SamplerOptions.dd_sequence field is defined but never read anywhere in the execution path. Silently ignored option. 

69. SamplerOptions.skip_transpilation field is defined but never read anywhere in the execution path. Silently ignored option. 

70. SamplerOptions.optimization_level field is defined but never read anywhere in the execution path. Silently ignored option. 

71. EstimatorOptions struct is defined but never used anywhere in the file. Dead code. 

72. ZNEExtrapolator enum is defined but never used anywhere in the file. Dead code. 

73. DDSequence enum is used only as a field type in SamplerOptions and ErrorMitigationConfig, neither of which has its DD fields consumed. Effectively dead. 

74. Observable.pauliY creates an observable with Pauli Y string "Y" but coefficient (1.0, 0.0). The Pauli Y matrix has purely imaginary eigenvalues in the matrix sense but in Pauli operator notation the expectation value is real. However, the coefficient imaginary part is 0.0, and the computation in computeExpectationValue only uses coefficient.re — so the imaginary part of any complex coefficient is always ignored. This makes complex observables impossible to correctly represent. 

75. IBMQuantumClient.init: If initializeDefaultBackends() fails partway through (e.g., after sim is created but before heron is created), the alreadyinserted backends are in the map. The errdefer on client only calls allocator.destroy(client), NOT client.deinit(). So all partiallyinserted backends are leaked. 

76. initializeDefaultBackends: If self.backends.put(sim_name, sim) fails (OOM), sim_name is leaked and sim is leaked. 

77. initializeDefaultBackends: If self.backends.put(heron_name, heron) fails, heron_name and heron are leaked. 

78. initializeDefaultBackends: If self.backends.put(eagle_name, eagle) fails, eagle_name and eagle are leaked. 

79. initializeDefaultBackends: self.default_backend = "ibmq_qasm_simulator" sets a string literal pointer, not a heapallocated string. But in deinit, there is no free call for default_backend — this is correct since it's a literal. However, if default_backend is ever set to a heapallocated string elsewhere, it would be leaked. The inconsistency in ownership is a design flaw. 

80. authenticate: self.token_expiry = @as(i64, @intCast(std.time.nanoTimestamp())) +| QuantumConfig.TOKEN_VALIDITY_MS — nanoTimestamp() returns nanoseconds, but TOKEN_VALIDITY_MS is 3,600,000 (milliseconds). Adding milliseconds to a nanosecond timestamp produces a semantically wrong token_expiry — the token will appear to expire approximately 3.6 seconds after creation (3,600,000 nanoseconds = 3.6 ms into the future), not 1 hour. 

81. isAuthenticated: @as(i64, @intCast(std.time.nanoTimestamp())) < self.token_expiry — same unit mismatch as above. The comparison of a nanosecond timestamp to a value that was computed as nanoTimestamp() + milliseconds is wrong. 

82. authenticate: If self.access_token is already set from a previous authenticate() call, the old token string is never freed before assigning the new one — memory leak on reauthentication. 

83. authenticate: If self.session_id is already set, same memory leak on reauthentication. 

84. listBackends: Returns a [][]const u8 that the caller owns (allocated via self.allocator.alloc), but nowhere in the file is the returned slice freed by any caller. There is also no documented ownership transfer. The returned slice will be leaked by any caller. 

85. runCircuit: The backend variable is ?*QuantumBackend (optional). The check if (backend == null) is done, then backend.? is used later. But between the null check and the use, self.authenticate() is called which can fail — no issue with the backend null safety. However, if QuantumJob.init fails (try QuantumJob.init(...)), the function returns an error. But the job was not yet added to active_jobs, so no cleanup needed there. This is fine. 

86. runCircuit: If self.active_jobs.put(job_key, job) fails, job_key is leaked and job is leaked (the allocated QuantumJob is never freed). 

87. runCircuit: If self.executeJob(job, circuit, backend.?, options) fails after the job was inserted into active_jobs, the job remains in the map in a potentially partial/inconsistent state (status = RUNNING, no result). There is no rollback mechanism. 

88. runCircuit: const actual_backend_name = backend_name orelse self.default_backend.? — if backend_name is null AND self.default_backend is null, this panics with an unwrap of null. The earlier code handles the case where the backend was not found, but default_backend being null is separately possible (e.g., after construction but before initializeDefaultBackends). 

89. executeJob: result.execution_time_ms = job.end_time.? - job.start_time.? — the field is named execution_time_ms but the values stored are nanosecond timestamps subtracted from each other. The result is in nanoseconds, not milliseconds. Wrong unit. 

90. executeJob: If simulateCircuit or executeOnHardware returns an error, result (the QuantumResult) that was already allocated is never freed — memory leak. 

91. simulateCircuit: const dim = @as(usize, 1) << @intCast(@min(n, QuantumConfig.MAX_QUBITS_SIMULATION)) — if n == 0 (zeroqubit circuit), dim = 1. The probabilities array has 1 element and the simulation runs, generating a single bitstring of length 0 (bits = 0). The while loop while (bit_idx < bits) never executes, bitstring_len stays 0, and bitstring = bitstring_buf[0..0] is an empty slice. result.counts.get("") is called, which could produce unexpected behavior. 

92. simulateCircuit: The simulation completely ignores the actual circuit.instructions. The circuit content (which gates were applied, what state was prepared) has zero effect on the probability distribution. The "simulation" is purely random noise — this is a fundamental logical error that makes the simulator physically meaningless. 

93. simulateCircuit: val >>= 1 on a usize — if outcome (and thus val) is 0, this is fine. But val is of type usize (the type of outcome), and rightshifting is defined. The issue is that val is never reused correctly because bitstring_len = bits is set inside the loop on every iteration instead of once before the loop — redundant but not buggy per se. 

94. simulateCircuit: The count update for existing bitstrings uses a linear scan through the hash map (while (counts_iter.next()) |entry| { if (std.mem.eql(...)) { entry.value_ptr.* = current + 1; break; } }). This is O(n) per shot where n is the number of distinct outcomes. A correct approach would be to use result.counts.getPtr(bitstring) directly. This is a severe performance bug for large shot counts. 

95. simulateCircuit: The same linear scan pattern exists in executeOnHardware — same performance bug. 

96. simulateCircuit: bitstring_buf is a stacklocal buffer. When result.addCount(bitstring, 1) is called, addCount calls self.allocator.dupe(u8, bitstring) — so the key is properly heapcopied. But the result.counts.get(bitstring) call uses the stack pointer, which is valid for the duration of the loop iteration. This is technically safe but fragile. 

97. executeOnHardware: Same issue as 92 — the actual circuit instructions are completely ignored. Only getDepth() and countTwoQubitGates() are called for fidelity estimation, but the actual quantum state produced by the gates is not simulated. 

98. executeOnHardware: The noise model is p.* = base_p * fidelity + noise where noise = (1.0 - fidelity) * random.float(f64). This means the probability of outcome 0 is doubled (if (hw_prob_idx == 0) { p.* *= 2.0; }). This introduces a systematic bias toward the |0⟩ state that is physically unjustified and not based on any real noise model. 

99. executeOnHardware: If fidelity is negative (which can happen if avg_gate_error > 1.0 or avg_readout_error > 1.0, unlikely but possible with malformed calibration data), base_p * fidelity produces a negative probability. The normalization later may or may not fix this depending on the sum. 

100. waitForJob: The timeout_ms parameter name implies milliseconds, but start and the comparison use nanoTimestamp() values in nanoseconds. The comparison @as(i64, @intCast(nanoTimestamp())) - start > timeout_ms compares nanoseconds elapsed against milliseconds, so the timeout fires after timeout_ms nanoseconds (microsecondsscale), not milliseconds. 

101. waitForJob: If the job is already terminal when waitForJob is called, the while (!job.isTerminal()) loop is never entered and the function returns immediately — this is correct behavior, but the timeout check is never validated. Fine. 

102. createGrover: @as(u64, 1) << @intCast(num_qubits) — if num_qubits >= 64, this is an undefined shift overflow. For num_qubits == 64, 1 << 64 is undefined behavior / panic. No guard on num_qubits maximum value. 

103. createGrover: The oracle implementation uses a chain of CX gates (controlledX from each control to the target) as an approximation of a multicontrolledX (Toffoli). This is not a correct multicontrolled gate — it implements a series of independent CNOTs, not a single CCX with all controls simultaneously required. The Grover oracle is logically wrong for num_qubits > 2. 

104. createGrover: The diffusion operator similarly uses a chain of CX gates rather than a true multicontrolled gate. Same logical error as 103. 

105. createGrover: num_iterations is computed as @intFromFloat(@floor(std.math.pi / 4.0 * @sqrt(...))). For num_qubits == 0, @sqrt(1.0) = 1.0, pi/4 * 1 ≈ 0.785, @floor(0.785) = 0, num_iterations = 0. The initialization loop runs 0 times. The circuit is empty. No panic, but the result is a meaningless empty circuit. 

106. createGrover: For num_qubits == 1, @as(u64, 1) << 1 = 2, @sqrt(2.0) ≈ 1.414, pi/4 * 1.414 ≈ 1.11, @floor = 1.0, num_iterations = 1. The oracle and diffusion are entered, but the if (num_qubits >= 2) block is skipped — so the oracle applies X gates but the phase kickback / Grover operator is never applied. The Grover iteration is incomplete for singlequbit case. 

107. createVQEAnsatz: The entanglement loop while (ent_idx < num_qubits - 1) — if num_qubits == 0, then num_qubits - 1 wraps around to std.math.maxInt(usize) (usize underflow), causing an essentially infinite loop. No guard on num_qubits == 0. 

108. createVQEAnsatz: Same underflow issue in createQAOA with while (cost_idx < num_qubits - 1) for the case num_qubits == 0. 

109. createQFT: The QFT implementation applies controlledRZ gates as rz(j, angle); cx(i, j); rz(j, -angle); cx(i, j). This is the decomposition of a controlledphase gate (CP gate) into CX and RZ. However, the standard QFT uses controlledphase gates (P or CP), not controlledRZ. The CRZ gate is different from CP; CRZ applies Rz(θ) to the target controlled on the control qubit, while CP applies a phase to the |11⟩ state. The QFT implemented here is mathematically incorrect. 

110. createQFT: No guard on num_qubits == 0 — the outer loop doesn't execute, but measureAll() is called on a zeroqubit circuit, which is harmless. However, the swap phase while (swap_idx < num_qubits / 2) with num_qubits = 0 gives 0 / 2 = 0, so the loop doesn't run. Fine here. 

111. computeExpectationValue: if (q < bitstring.len and bitstring[bitstring.len - 1 - q] == '1') — q is of type u32 and bitstring.len is usize. The comparison q < bitstring.len is valid (implicit coercion). However, bitstring.len - 1 - q can underflow if q >= bitstring.len — but this is guarded by the left side of the and. However, if bitstring.len == 0, then bitstring.len - 1 - q wraps to a huge usize even for q = 0 if the guard fails. With bitstring.len == 0, q < bitstring.len is q < 0 which is always false for u32. So it is guarded. Fine. 

112. computeGradient: exp_plus and exp_minus are computed by calling computeExpectationValue twice on the same unchanged circuit — the result is always the same value. The gradient is always (x - x) / 2 = 0. The parameter shift rule requires running the circuit with param_idxth parameter shifted by +π/2 and -π/2 respectively, but this is not implemented. computeGradient is completely broken — always returns 0. 

113. computeGradient: param_idx is accepted as a parameter and immediately discarded with _ = param_idx. The function ignores which parameter to differentiate with respect to. 

114. QuantumClassicalHybridOptimizer.init: errdefer is missing on the optimizer allocation. If anything after allocator.create(Self) fails, optimizer is leaked. In the current code nothing between create and return can fail, but this is fragile. 

115. IBMQuantumClient has a getBackend function that takes *Self (mutable pointer) but doesn't mutate anything — it should be *const Self. 

116. listBackends takes *Self but doesn't mutate — should be *const Self. 

117. The QuantumBackend fields pending_jobs and queue_position are always initialized to 0 and never updated anywhere in the code. They are dead fields that carry no real information. 

118. QuantumBackend.status is always set to .ONLINE at construction time and never updated. No mechanism exists to transition backend status. The BackendStatus enum variants OFFLINE, MAINTENANCE, CALIBRATING, RESERVED are effectively dead. 

119. QuantumJob.circuits_count is always set to 1 in runCircuit, regardless of how many circuits might be run. The field is never used after initialization. Dead. 

120. QuantumJob.queue_position and estimated_wait_seconds are always 0 and never updated. Dead fields. 

121. QuantumResult.quasi_distributions is initialized as an empty ArrayList and never populated anywhere in the code. Always empty — dead field. 

122. QuantumResult.memory is always null — never populated. Dead field. 

123. QuantumResult.metadata (in QuantumResult) is always empty — never populated. Dead field. 

124. QuantumCircuit.metadata is always empty — never populated. Dead field. 

125. QuantumCircuit.global_phase is always 0.0 — never updated. Dead field. 

126. QuantumCondition struct is defined and referenced as the type of QuantumInstruction.condition, but condition is always null — conditional gates are never created. Dead. 

127. QuantumInstruction.init sets classical_bits = &[_]u32{} (empty slice literal). In deinit, if (self.classical_bits.len > 0) self.allocator.free(self.classical_bits) — this is correct since we don't free the literal. But it means instructions created via init cannot have classical bits set later without a redesign. 

128. barrier method in QuantumCircuit: calls QuantumInstruction.init(self.allocator, .BARRIER, qubits, &[_]f64{}) — qubits is a []const u8 passed in from the caller. Inside init, try allocator.dupe(u32, qubits) dupes the slice. However, qubits in the barrier signature is []const u32 — callerowned data is duped, correct. But the caller is responsible for not passing a dangling pointer, which is fine. No issue here per se. 

129. Test "circuit execution on simulator": const job = try client.runCircuit(...) — the job is stored in client.active_jobs. The client.deinit() via defer will clean up the job. But circuit.deinit() is also deferred and runs before client.deinit() (defer is LIFO). The circuit is freed before the job is completed — but execution is synchronous, so the circuit is only accessed during runCircuit, which completes before any defer runs. Fine. 

130. Test "quantum circuit creation": try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 6), circuit.instructions.items.len) — the circuit has: h(0), cx(0,1), cx(1,2), and measureAll() which adds 3 measures (one per qubit). Total = 6. This is correct and the test passes. No error here. 

131. Test "quantum circuit depth calculation": try std.testing.expect(depth >= 2) — this is a weak assertion. With h(0), h(1) (parallel, depth 1), then cx(0,1) (depth 2), the actual depth is 2. The test passes for any depth ≥ 2, so even if depth were computed as 1000, the test would pass. The test doesn't verify correctness, only a lower bound. 

132. Test "IBM quantum client authentication": try std.testing.expect(client.isAuthenticated()) — this test will fail due to the unit mismatch bug in item 80. The token_expiry is set to nanoTimestamp() + 3_600_000, meaning it expires ~3.6ms after setting. By the time isAuthenticated() is called, the token is likely already expired. The test is flawed and will intermittently or consistently fail. 

133. IBMQuantumClient.deinit: self.credentials.deinit() is called, which calls self.allocator.destroy(self) on the credentials struct. But self.credentials is a *IBMQuantumCredentials — the pointer is allocated on the heap. After credentials.deinit(), the pointer is invalid. Then self.allocator.destroy(self) frees the IBMQuantumClient itself. The allocator stored in credentials and the one in client are the same, so no crossallocator issue. This is correct sequencing. 

134. simulateCircuit and executeOnHardware are nearly identical in structure (probability array generation, shot sampling, bitstring construction, count update). The entire countupdate and bitstringgeneration block is duplicated verbatim — significant code duplication that should be extracted to a helper function. 

135. toOpenQASM3: The else branch catches all gates not explicitly handled (including ID, Y, Z, S, SDG, T, TDG, SX, SXDG). For multiqubit variants of these that may exist, the else branch accesses inst.qubits[0] — if a Y gate were somehow added with 0 qubits, it panics. More importantly, Y, Z, S, etc. are valid singlequbit gates that correctly fall into else, but the else branch would also catch any future gate incorrectly if it requires more than 1 qubit or parameter. 

136. QuantumBackend.initHardwareWithCalibration: After if (owns_calibration) { calibration.deinit(); }, the backend.* = Self{...} assignment contains try allocator.dupe(u8, name). If this fails, the function returns an error. At this point, t1, t2, readout_err, coupling are protected by errdefers. But basis (allocated earlier) has no errdefer — confirmed memory leak. 

137. QuantumBackend fields t1_times_ns, t2_times_ns, readout_errors, gate_errors, coupling_map, basis_gates are typed as []const (immutable slices), but are allocated as mutable slices and then cast. This is fine in Zig. But in deinit, self.allocator.free(self.coupling_map) requires a mutable slice — Zig's free accepts []const T as well via the allocator interface. Fine. 

138. The QuantumBackend struct stores basis_gates: []const []const u8. In deinit, self.allocator.free(self.basis_gates) frees the outer slice but not the inner string slices. For simulator backends, the inner strings are literals — correct. For hardware backends, same. But if the basis_gates array were ever populated with heapallocated strings, there would be a leak. 

139. createGHZState: The loop while (ghz_idx < num_qubits) with ghz_idx: usize = 1 and num_qubits: u32 — implicit comparison between usize and u32. Zig performs implicit integer coercion in comparisons, so ghz_idx < num_qubits compiles. But if num_qubits = 0, then ghz_idx (1) < num_qubits (0) is false, so the loop doesn't run. h(0) was called on a 0qubit circuit (num_qubits = 0 means qubit 0 doesn't exist) — outofbounds qubit index, which is not validated. 

140. createGHZState: The circuit is initialized with num_qubits qubits and num_qubits classical bits. measureAll measures @min(num_qubits, num_classical_bits) = num_qubits qubits. Correct. 

141. createQAOA: The QAOA cost layer applies cx(cost_idx, cost_idx + 1); rz(cost_idx + 1, 0.0); cx(cost_idx, cost_idx + 1) — all RZ parameters are hardcoded to 0.0. A rotation by 0 does nothing. The QAOA cost and mixer angles (gamma and beta) are variational parameters that should be inputs to the function, not hardcoded zeros. The circuit is structurally a QAOA but functionally identity (all rotation angles are zero). 

142. createVQEAnsatz: Same issue — all RY and RZ angles are 0.0. The VQE ansatz with allzero parameters is an identity circuit. 

143. createQFT: No validation that num_qubits <= QuantumConfig.HERON_QUBITS or similar — a user can create a QFT for more qubits than any backend supports, and the circuit is happily constructed. 

144. IBMQuantumCredentials.parseCRN: If the CRN string doesn't contain enough colons to reach index 5, 6, or 7, parts.next() simply returns null and those fields remain as their initial values (region = DEFAULT_REGION, account_id = "", resource_id = ""). No error is returned for a malformed CRN. 

145. parseCRN: account_id is initialized as "" (empty string literal, not heapallocated). But in deinit, if (self.account_id.len > 0) self.allocator.free(self.account_id) — the check prevents freeing the literal. However, if the account parsing sets account_id to a nonempty heap string, but then a subsequent dupe in the same function fails and errdefer allocator.destroy(creds) fires, account_id is leaked (it's heapallocated but not registered in any errdefer). 

146. parseCRN: resource_id has the same leak potential as account_id — initialized as "", conditionally heapallocated, but not protected by errdefer. 

147. getDepth is declared as returning u32 but uses std.AutoHashMap(u32, u32).init(self.allocator). This hash map allocates and defer qubit_depths.deinit() cleans it up. But getDepth is a *const Self method — using self.allocator is valid. The issue is this method can fail internally (allocator failure in put) but the error is silently swallowed. 

148. QuantumResult.addCount: try self.counts.put(key, count) — if put fails after key was duped, key is leaked because the errdefer from the failed put doesn't free the key. Actually: const key = try self.allocator.dupe(u8, bitstring) succeeds, then try self.counts.put(key, count) fails — key is leaked. 

149. QuantumResult.deinit: Only the keys of counts are freed (self.allocator.free(entry.key_ptr.*)). The values are u64 primitives — no heap allocation, nothing to free. Correct. 

150. QuantumBackend.estimateFidelity: The circuit_depth parameter is used to compute depth_factor = exp(-depth / 100). If circuit_depth = 0, depth_factor = exp(0) = 1.0. The fidelity = gate_fidelity * readout_fidelity * 1.0. This is correct for a zerodepth circuit, but a zerodepth circuit with gates has no logical meaning. No validation. 

That's all.
